findings.headline: From 1 April 2027, the council will restrict permanent recruitment to essential posts only; senior management will shift to temporary or shared arrangements
findings.detail: The council has committed to hiring permanent staff only where essential for service delivery or LGR support from April 2027 onwards. Senior management posts will transition to temporary arrangements or resource-sharing with other councils. This represents a material tightening of staffing discretion and capacity during the final nine months before vesting.
findings.matters: Severe restrictions on recruitment and temporary management structures during final transition months create operational risk - reduced institutional knowledge, potential service continuity issues, and limited decision-making capacity at a critical time.
findings.figures: Staffing restrictions effective 1 April 2027 through vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: From 1 April 2027, the Council expects to only undertake permanent recruitment to any vacant post where it is essential for the delivery of services. From 1 April 2027, for senior management posts – the Council expects to use temporary arrangements or, where possible, seek to share resources with other Councils.

findings.headline: From late 2026/early 2027, a Section 24 regime will require Shadow Council consent for major financial commitments above set thresholds
findings.detail: The Structural Changes Order will trigger Section 24 directions requiring the Shadow Council's formal consent for decisions exceeding specified thresholds: land disposals over £100k, capital contracts over £1m, and revenue contracts over £100k with impacts extending beyond vesting day. This creates a consent-based governance framework that will constrain the council's financial decision-making until 1 April 2028.
findings.matters: Section 24 restrictions could delay or prevent necessary financial or capital decisions during the critical transition period, reducing operational flexibility when it is most needed. Their imposition also signals government concern about financial stability risks.
findings.figures: Land disposals > £100,000; Capital contracts > £1,000,000; Revenue contracts > £100,000 whole-life cost
findings.quote: Once the SCO is in place and the Section 24 Direction is issued certain decisions by predecessor councils will require the consent of the Shadow Council. Thresholds for consent commonly include: Land disposals > £100,000. Capital contracts > £1,000,000. Revenue contracts > £100,000 (whole life cost), where they extend beyond vesting day.

findings.headline: The council will rely on drawing down the Financial Sustainability Reserve to cover projected budget deficits rather than making structural spending adjustments
findings.detail: The council's reserve strategy explicitly commits to using the Financial Sustainability Reserve to cover the projected revenue gaps (£0.831m in 2027/28 and £1.531m in 2028/29). This approach treats the reserve as a temporary buffer for recurring structural imbalances rather than making cuts or finding permanent solutions to budget gaps. The FSR balance will consequently shrink from £2.798m to £1.446m.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing deficits is unsustainable - it masks structural problems rather than solving them, potentially forcing abrupt decisions on the new unitary council immediately after vesting if the FSR is insufficient.
findings.figures: FSR projected to cover £0.831m (2027/28) and £1.531m (2028/29) deficits
findings.quote: Fund projected gaps ("deficits") in the MTFP via the Financial Sustainability Reserve to balance the budget

findings.headline: Total usable reserves will decline from £15.3m to £4.6m by March 2028, a 70% reduction driven by committed spending
findings.detail: The council plans significant drawdowns of earmarked reserves over the next two years. The Erewash Investment Fund (both tranches totalling £6.372m) will be fully deployed to complete committed projects. The £2m LGR reserve will fund transition costs. Additional reserves for Local Plan, Digital Transformation, and other purposes will also be exhausted. The Financial Sustainability Reserve will decline from £2.798m to £1.446m.
findings.matters: The incoming unitary council will inherit a heavily depleted reserve position with minimal flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures, service demands, or transition impacts - leaving it operationally and financially vulnerable.
findings.figures: Total usable reserves: £15,316k (1 April 2026) → £4,606k (31 March 2028); Erewash Investment Fund: £6.372k → £0; Financial Sustainability Reserve: £2.798k → £1.446k
findings.quote: The EIF is fully allocated with funds held in reserves until spent.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial forecasts have deteriorated significantly, with budget gaps nearly doubling for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's projected revenue gap for 2027/28 has increased from £0.420m (reported when the 2026/27 budget was approved) to £0.831m - nearly a 100% increase. The 2028/29 gap has also worsened from £1.120m to £1.531m. The council acknowledges this position reflects additional emerging pressures and is likely to change again as 2026/27 performance is monitored.
findings.matters: Deteriorating budget forecasts indicate structural imbalances will be inherited by the new unitary council, potentially requiring immediate spending decisions or further reserve drawdowns immediately post-vesting.
findings.quote: Members will note that the position has moved compared to that reported when the budget was approved as additional pressures are envisaged for 2027/28. This position will likely change again as budget performance for 2026/27 is monitored.

findings.headline: New cost pressures identified post-budget with no allocation, council relying on underspends to manage
findings.detail: Since the 2026/27 budget was set in March, new costs have been identified: insurance contract £50k more than forecast, health and safety measures (dashcams, workshop pit covers, Long Eaton Town Hall safety), cyber insurance costs higher than expected and requiring additional security investment, and workforce training for LGR preparation. The council states it will manage these from underspends and additional income.
findings.matters: Emerging costs without budget provision indicate tighter financial headroom. Success depends on forecast underspends and income upside materialising, particularly investment income which is higher than budget due to interest rate assumptions.
findings.figures: Insurance increase: £0.050m. Investment income forecast upside: c£0.25m – c£0.4m
findings.quote: In other budgets, as at the of June, several new pressures have emerged since the budget was set these include: Insurance contract – The actual value of the contract was £0.050m more than forecast mainly on vehicles insurance.

findings.headline: Pay award inflation risk: union rejected 3.3% offer and is balloting for strike action
findings.detail: National Employers offered all staff 3.3% for 2026/27, but unions rejected this offer and are balloting members for strike action. The council budgeted for 3%, and every 1 percentage point variance costs or saves the council £0.120m.
findings.matters: Unresolved pay negotiations with strike action balloting create cost inflation risk and operational disruption. At worst, a gap of 1.3% between offer and budget would cost the council £0.156m without mitigation.
findings.figures: Budget assumption: 3%. Employer offer: 3.3%. Cost per 1% variance: c£0.120m
findings.quote: National Employers have offered 3.3% to all staff for the annual pay award for 2026/27. The Trade Unions have rejected this offer and are now balloting members for strike action over the summer... The Council have budgeted for a pay award of 3%. Every 1% variance to that budgeted would cost/save the Council c£0.120m.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve reduced to £2m, down 54% from £4.3m, through deliberate repurposing
findings.detail: The council reduced its unallocated General Fund balance from £4.327m to £2.0m as part of a deliberate policy repurposing approved by the Council. This leaves reduced headroom for managing future budget shocks or unexpected pressures. The council still carries £12.2m in earmarked reserves for specific purposes.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial resilience through unallocated reserves. A 54% reduction in the General Fund narrows the council's buffer for absorbing unexpected costs or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: General Fund balance 1 April 2025: £4.327m. General Fund balance 31 March 2026: £2.000m. Deliberate repurposing: £2.327m
findings.quote: Balance brought forward 1 April 2025 4,327 [£000s]; Repurposing of General Fund (Council Executive, July 2025) (2,327); Balance carried forward at 31 March 2026 2,000

findings.paper_title: 2. Appendix 1 - Reserves Policy 2027 Budget Strategy FINAL
findings.headline: Capital programme funding from receipts runs out in March 2028; land sale of £1.257m deferred from 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council relies on capital receipts to fund parts of the capital programme. Land sales forecast for 2025/26 have been deferred to 2026/27, and the council forecasts capital receipts will fund the capital programme only through March 2028.
findings.matters: March 2028 is a defined end-point for capital receipt funding; beyond that date the council must find alternative funding (borrowing or grants) for capital spending, constraining future capital programme flexibility.
findings.figures: £1.257m land sale deferral, capital receipts funding through March 2028
findings.quote: £1.257m of land sales which were forecast to be received in 2025/26 are now forecast to be received in 2026/27. The council is forecasting to have enough capital receipts to finance its capital programme through to March 2028.

findings.paper_title: 2. Appendix 1 - Reserves Policy 2027 Budget Strategy FINAL
findings.headline: LGR transformation can be funded from £2m LGR Reserve or up to £2.798m drawn from Financial Sustainability Reserve, depleting deficit-backing reserves
findings.detail: The council has a separate £2m LGR reserve for Local Government Reorganisation. The FSR balance could also be transferred to support transformations and viability in the early years, meaning both reserves could be deployed during reorganisation and unavailable as a buffer.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change; if FSR must be drawn for transformation costs, the council loses its buffer against budget deficits during a period of organisational change.
findings.figures: £2m LGR Reserve, £2.798m Financial Sustainability Reserve
findings.quote: In the context of LGR, the balance could be transferred to support transformations and viability in the early years.

findings.paper_title: 2. Appendix 1 - Reserves Policy 2027 Budget Strategy FINAL
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability Reserve of £2.798m established to hold balances equivalent to projected deficits from the Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.detail: The council created this reserve specifically to enable it to balance its budget whilst taking action to make savings and generate income. This indicates the MTFP contains projected budget deficits requiring financial backing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's projected deficits are temporary or structural, and whether the reserve is sufficient to cover them without requiring additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £2.798m Financial Sustainability Reserve
findings.quote: The Council has a Financial Sustainability Reserve which was established to hold balances equivalent to the projected deficits per the MTFP. This would allow the Council the scope to balance its budget whilst it took action to make savings and/or generate income.

findings.headline: Investment income exceeded budget by £196,272 due to higher interest rates and capital underspend
findings.detail: Interest receivable totalled £1,396,272 against a budget of £1,200,000, with the favorable variance driven by interest rates staying higher than forecast and higher cash balances from slower capital programme delivery. The council achieved an average return of 4.092% on £31.037m average balance.
findings.matters: Strong treasury management and above-budget income demonstrates financial competence and provides additional revenue to support budget sustainability.
findings.figures: Budgeted interest £1,200,000; Actual £1,396,272; Variance £196,272 favorable; Average return 4.092%
findings.quote: The actual amount received and accrued for the year was £1,396,272 resulting in a favourable variance of £196,272.

findings.headline: Council remains debt-free with zero borrowing requirement in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) remains at £0m for both opening and closing positions. All £9.927m of capital expenditure was financed through capital grants, receipts and reserves, with no external borrowing from PWLB or money markets.
findings.matters: A debt-free position indicates strong financial health and flexibility for lenders assessing credit risk and the council's capacity for future borrowing.
findings.figures: CFR opening £0m; CFR closing £0m; Capital financed entirely from grants, receipts and reserves (£9.927m)
findings.quote: The Council had no borrowing requirement during the year 2025/26 and remains debt free.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered at 40% of planned spend due to Towns Fund project delays
findings.detail: The council originally planned capital expenditure of £24.628m for 2025/26, revised mid-year to £10.477m, with actual outturn at £9.927m. The shortfall is explicitly attributed to delays in Towns Fund project delivery. This represents a material implementation challenge.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery is critical for lenders assessing whether a council can execute planned investments, especially schemes with government conditions or time constraints. Significant underspend signals implementation risk.
findings.figures: Original estimate £24.628m; Revised estimate £10.477m; Actual spend £9.927m
findings.quote: As indicated in 3.8b above, delays in delivery of the Towns Fund projects meant capital expenditure defrayed was lower than expected.

findings.headline: Town Deal £25m delivery programme explicitly identified as carrying 'potentially significant financial risk'
findings.detail: The council holds £25m Department for Levelling Up funding for Long Eaton Town Deal and serves as the accountable body. The statement explicitly states the delivery is 'not without potentially significant financial risk' with three categories: budget/cost overruns, timescales (March 2026 government deadline), and value-for-money compliance. As of May 2025 projects were expected to complete within budget, but deadline risk remains.
findings.matters: The council bears accountability for £25m of government funding. Budget overruns or delivery failures would require the council to either fund the gap or absorb costs, directly impacting council finances.
findings.figures: £25m investment; March 2026 government deadline
findings.quote: The delivery of the Town Deal is not without potentially significant financial risk for the council. There are three key risks: 1. Budget/Cost – projects costing more than available budget; 2. Timescales – projects not completing before end of March 2026; 3. Value for money

findings.headline: Financial performance section of Annual Governance Statement incomplete with placeholder text
findings.detail: The 'Financial performance and resilience' section of this governance statement contains only placeholder text '~~ INSERT TEXT ~~' marked 'to be completed once available'. Similarly, the 'Corporate performance' section is marked 'to update once Q4 performance data captured'. These are unusual omissions from a formal governance statement being formally presented to the Audit Committee.
findings.matters: Financial performance disclosure is fundamental to a governance statement. Incomplete disclosure at point of committee approval raises questions about the timeliness and quality of financial reporting controls.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Financial performance and resilience     to be completed once available ~~ INSERT TEXT ~~

findings.headline: External auditors disclaimed opinion on financial statements for year ended 31 March 2025
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars LLP presented their Auditors Annual Report to the Audit Committee in February 2026. The report included a disclaimed opinion on the financial statements, meaning the auditors could not form an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view. This stands in contrast to the council's own assessment that its internal control environment provides 'Reasonable Assurance'.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion on financial statements is a material audit finding that undermines confidence in the council's reported financial position. Lenders depend on audited financial statements for credit assessment and covenant monitoring.
findings.figures: Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: their Auditors Annual Report for the year ended 31 st March 2025 which included a disclaimed opinion on the financial statements

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Appendix 1, Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Outsourced audit partner CMAP's resourcing problems required 4 audits to be deferred and a firm change for 2026/27
findings.detail: Four planned audits (Asset Registers, Licensing, Contracting procedures, and Financial Accounting Ledger) were deferred from 2025/26 due to capacity issues with the council's then-outsourced audit provider CMAP. The council has now replaced them with BDO for 2026/27, but the deferral creates a gap in year-on-year audit continuity.
findings.matters: Gaps in audit coverage reduce the council's ability to identify emerging control weaknesses, and changes to audit firms can disrupt the effectiveness of oversight.
findings.figures: 4 audits deferred; 1 audit incomplete at year end (Section 106 Monies)
findings.quote: Work in progress and deferred work primarily arises from resourcing challenges with our out-sourced partner CMAP.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Appendix 1, Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Two medium-graded audit recommendations are overdue against their agreed completion dates
findings.detail: Of 16 open audit recommendations at year-end, 2 medium-graded actions are recorded as 'overdue against latest agreed date'. The paper states these are 'not considered to be a risk', but they represent missed internal deadlines for addressing control gaps that auditors ranked as material enough to require medium-graded remediation.
findings.matters: Overdue audit recommendations indicate the council is slower than planned in fixing known control weaknesses, prolonging the period of exposure to identified risks.
findings.figures: 16 open actions at year-end: 0 high, 6 medium (of which 2 overdue, 3 with extended dates), 10 low
findings.quote: Overdue against latest agreed date 0 2 0

findings.paper_title: Item 5 Appendix 1, Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Audit opinion is 'Reasonable', not 'Substantial', indicating some control gaps remain
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit gave a 'Reasonable Assurance' opinion rather than Substantial. Under the audit definitions stated in this paper, Reasonable means 'some may not be fully effective. A small number of exceptions found in testing'. The paper states no 'significant' control failures were identified, but the Reasonable rating explicitly indicates weaknesses in the council's control environment.
findings.matters: A Reasonable rather than Substantial assurance opinion means there are known gaps in financial or operational controls that creditors need to account for when assessing the council's reliability.
findings.figures: 0 audits gave 'Limited' or 'No' assurance; overall opinion dropped to Reasonable despite 11 audits being performed
findings.quote: All audits performed in the year resulted in Reasonable or Substantial Assurance, indicating sound control environments across the areas reviewed.

findings.headline: Structural recruitment and retention crisis across multiple services affecting service capacity and forcing agency use
findings.detail: The council reports unable to recruit at competitive rates in: drivers (dedicated recruitment and retention programme at £18k), Planning Enforcement (resorting to agency at £35,000 for one person), Property and Estates Manager (multiple failed attempts requiring restructure), and Property Officer (retiring early requiring handover costs). This pattern suggests systematic wage gaps versus the market.
findings.matters: Inability to recruit or retain staff either reduces service quality or forces permanent cost increases; both damage financial sustainability. Agency costs are higher and non-recurring
findings.figures: £35,000 (Planning Enforcement agency staffing); £18,000 (driver recruitment and retention programme); £113,880 (pay and grading review including national scale changes); £52,060 (Legal restructure to retain staff in qualified positions)
findings.quote: The Council has struggled to recruit and retain drivers in a competitive market where all other local authorities are also recruiting due to the new implementation of Food Waste service

findings.headline: Debt recovery function cut then reported unsustainable, now requiring urgent restaffing at £164k
findings.detail: The council reduced debt recovery capacity by over 2 FTE posts (approximately £90k) in 2024/25 after pandemic recovery efforts, then now faces an acute capacity crisis: 'more debt is now reaching Liability Order stage (i.e. payments are not being made following a Reminder Letter)'. The position is reported as 'unsustainable'. The council is now adding 2 Late Recovery Officers and 2 Revenue Officers to restore capacity.
findings.matters: Inability to collect debt is an income leak and signals collection risk; the pattern of cutting capacity then having to backfill urgently suggests poor planning and indicates debts are harder to recover
findings.figures: £90k (capacity cut in 2024/25); £164,080 (restaffing pressure for 2026/27)
findings.quote: This position is now unsustainable as more debt is now reaching Liability Order stage (i.e. payments are not being made following a 'Reminder Letter').

findings.headline: Multiple earmarked reserves being drawn down to fund 2026/27 current operations
findings.detail: The council is explicitly using earmarked reserves to fund ongoing costs: Homelessness reserve to offset Renters Rights Act staffing (£272,710), ICT reserve for Arcus planning system (£40,000), and Erewash Investment Fund for free December car parking (£100,000). This pattern of reserve depletion to cover operational pressures rather than one-time costs suggests structural budget imbalance.
findings.matters: Using reserves for current operations is unsustainable; once reserves are depleted, the council must cut services, raise borrowing, or increase fees. It signals the underlying budget is in structural deficit
findings.figures: £412,710 total from named reserves in this document (Homelessness £272,710, ICT £40,000, EIF £100,000)
findings.quote: The Council will use funds retained in the Homelessness reserve to offset this cost in 26/27

findings.headline: Investment income falling £556k as cash balances decline through capital deployment on Town Deal
findings.detail: Investment income is forecast to fall by £556,820 due to expected interest rate reductions and a reduction in cash balances available for investment. The council attributes falling balances partly to increased expenditure 'particularly in relation to the Long Eaton Town Deal', indicating capital deployment is consuming reserves while operating income pressures mount simultaneously.
findings.matters: Liquidity is tightening: falling investment income coupled with capital deployment on Town Deal suggests cash buffers are eroding at a time when structural cost pressures (homelessness, food waste) are rising
findings.figures: £556,820 (investment income loss forecast); Long Eaton Town Deal identified as driver of balance reduction
findings.quote: reduction in balances invested as more expenditure is incurred particularly in relation to the Long Eaton Town Deal.

findings.headline: £936k unfunded annual cost for new food waste collection mandate with no identified revenue funding stream
findings.detail: New government legislation requires food waste collection from domestic properties from March 2026. The council has already spent just over £1m from capital (6 vehicles purchased) and must now budget £936,240 for ongoing operations including 10 loaders and 5 HGV drivers. The government confirmed funding is included in the Settlement but provided no separate new burdens revenue funding.
findings.matters: An unfunded mandate is a structural cost increase without corresponding revenue; it compresses margins and forces choices between funding this service or cutting others
findings.figures: £936,240 (annual revenue pressure for 2026/27); £1m+ (capital already spent on 6 vehicles); 10 loaders and 5 HGV drivers required
findings.quote: There will be no separate new burdens revenue funding with the Government confirming that funding is included in the Settlement.

findings.headline: Homelessness demand expected to persist indefinitely with no solution, compounded by loss of asylum dispersal grant funding
findings.detail: The council explicitly states there is 'no expectation that demand for service will decrease in the foreseeable future with limited availability of move on accommodation' and faces potential additional costs of up to £0.229m from private landlord provision alone. The Homelessness Asylum Dispersal Grant of £132,750 is no longer confirmed from 2026/27. Multiple staffing pressures reflect rising demand for housing advice and increasing temporary accommodation placements.
findings.matters: A growing, permanent demand with no exit strategy is a structural cost risk that will recur every year; coupled with lost grant funding, it threatens operating margins and forces reserve depletion
findings.figures: £272,710 (Renters Rights staffing); £132,750 (lost Asylum Dispersal Grant); potential additional £229,000 from private landlord accommodation; £39,330 + £28,980 (homelessness staffing pressures); £114,500 baseline supported accommodation with 50% contingency built in
findings.quote: There is no expectation that demand for service will decrease in the foreseeable future with limited availability of move on accommodation.

findings.headline: Council identifies supplier insolvency as medium risk due to economic conditions.
findings.detail: The financial risk assessment flags that the probability of suppliers going into liquidation is higher than in prior years due to current economic climate. The council performs financial checks on suppliers before contract award but acknowledges that future risk cannot be fully mitigated. Supplier defaults could delay or increase the cost of capital projects, which would further stress a financing position already constrained to reach March 2028.
findings.matters: Supplier failures could disrupt capital project delivery and create additional pressure on a capital programme that depends on planned land sales.
findings.figures: Risk level: MEDIUM RISK
findings.quote: Due to the general economic climate, the risk of suppliers going into liquidation is more probable than in prior years.

findings.headline: Council flags land sales as medium risk, with consequences for revenue budget if they fail to materialise.
findings.detail: The council's financial risk assessment (section 9.1) identifies capital receipts from land sales as medium risk. The council notes that timing and completion of sales are unpredictable due to external factors (offers, legal matters, market conditions), and if sales do not occur as forecast, the council would need to find alternative financing. The stated alternatives—revenue contribution to capital, borrowing, or leasing—all have adverse impacts on the revenue budget.
findings.matters: This signals to lenders that the council's capital financing depends on an uncertain income stream, and that contingency options would stress the revenue budget.
findings.figures: Forecast land sales: £4.406m in 2025/26 (£3.149m realised to 31 Dec), £0.355m in 2026/27, nil in 2027/28.
findings.quote: Should the land sales fail to occur as forecast then alternative ways of financing the essential capital expenditure would need to be found.

findings.headline: All capital receipts will be exhausted by 31 March 2028, leaving £46k available.
findings.detail: The proposed capital programme of £41.789m assumes capital receipts of £4.761m to fund projects. Current forecasts show capital receipts will decline to only £46k by end of March 2028. If the council executes its capital spending plan over the next two financial years, all capital receipts will be used. This transition occurs as Erewash ceases to exist and a new authority takes over on 1 April 2028.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can continue to finance essential capital expenditure after March 2028, or whether it will need to borrow or use revenue contributions.
findings.figures: Capital receipts forecast: 2025/26 (£1,586k), 2026/27 (£835k), 2027/28 (£46k). Land sales assumed: £4.761m, of which £3.149m already received in 2025/26.
findings.quote: if the Council defrays the sums allocated in the current revised 2025/26 Capital Programme and keeps to its capital spending plans over the course of the next two financial years, by the 31 March 2028 all of the Council's capital receipts will be utilised.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Recruitment and retention challenges: vacancy allowance increased to 6.5% with higher rates for new posts due to LGR competition
findings.detail: The council experienced higher-than-budgeted staff vacancies in 2025/26 (budgeted 5%, actual performance underperformed). Vacancy allowance increased to 6.5% for 2026/27 (£0.720m saving). For new posts being created (food waste, Renters Act, LGR support), service-specific vacancy allowances are higher to reflect slower recruitment. With LGR on the horizon and other councils recruiting for similar roles, recruitment challenges may worsen.
findings.matters: Sustained high vacancy levels could mean services cannot be delivered as planned. Conversely, being forced to hire expensively (agency staff) would breach budgets. This is a material budget uncertainty that will transfer to the new unitary.
findings.figures: Vacancy allowance budgeted 6.5% (£0.720m), up from 5%. New post vacancy allowance totals £0.265m (para 6.13, Risk 4)
findings.quote: Employee recruitment and retention continues to be challenging with in-year savings on the vacancy allowance budget of £0.525m at quarter 3 standing at £0.111m. The general vacancy rate has been increased from 5.0% to 6.5% which reduces the pay budget by £0.192m

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Finance system migration underway at cost of £0.132m with end-of-life risks if delayed past 2026/27
findings.detail: The council is replacing its current finance system (no longer supported by vendor) with the system used by Derby City Council. Revenue implementation costs estimated at up to £0.132m. The council is moving proactively to avoid forced migration later, but if implementation overruns, it will face system support cessation risk.
findings.matters: Finance system failures can disrupt reporting and controls. A lender would want to know the system is modern and supported. The migration risk is moderate but foreseeable.
findings.figures: Finance system implementation revenue costs up to £0.132m in 2026/27 (para 3.17)
findings.quote: Rather than "upgrade" its current system, the Council will use the opportunity to move to the system used by Derby City Council giving it greater resilience and preparing the ground for new arrangements under LGR. The expected costs have been updated and revenue costs of up to £0.132m are forecast to facilitate the implementation.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: New statutory duties (Renters Rights Act, food waste collection) funded by government but future funding and exact costs uncertain
findings.detail: The council must deliver new services from April 2026: mandatory weekly food waste collection (estimated £0.936m cost) and enhanced private rented sector enforcement under the Renters Rights Act. Government has provided capital funding for food waste but says the revenue costs are included in the settlement. For the Renters Act, only 2025/26 new burdens funding has been confirmed, with the government expecting enforcement fines to offset future costs. The council assumes zero fine income.
findings.matters: New burdens funded by assumptions about future settlement allocations and fine income create budget risk. If government funding does not materialise or fines do not reach expected levels, the council will face pressure. This risk transfers to the new unitary.
findings.figures: Food waste cost estimate £0.936m for staff and non-staff. Government capital funding £1.084851m for collection vehicles and caddies. Government allocated £312,476 transitional revenue funding for 2025/26 (Risk 14, para 4.31)
findings.quote: The Government assert that the funding for Waste Collection is included the Settlement so there has been no separate new burdens funding. The Council estimates costs at £0.936m for staff and non-staff costs which is similar to other district Councils.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Council Tax freeze maintained for 2026/27, eliminating £0.229m of potential revenue and limiting future flexibility
findings.detail: The council is freezing council tax at £220.22 per Band D property for 2026/27 (no increase). This politically popular decision forgoes £0.229m of potential revenue that a 2.99% increase would have yielded. Council tax is the largest single revenue source, and the continued freeze limits the council's future funding flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is constrained on its largest revenue source. With deficits emerging in 2027/28 and 2028/29, the inability to flex council tax (capped at 2.99% or £5 per year without referendum) is a material constraint. The new unitary may inherit the freeze expectation.
findings.figures: Council tax freeze loss of revenue £0.229m annually. Band D charge frozen at £220.22 (£4.24/week). Council tax revenue 2026/27 £7.668m on tax base of 34,820 (para 5.37)
findings.quote: the Executive is proposing that there should be no increase in the borough's Council Tax for 2026/27. The Council's charge for a Band D property will remain the same as that for 2025/26 at £220.22 (£4.24/week).

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Waste recycling contract volatility: force majeure notice served following processing plant fire
findings.detail: The council's waste recycling contractor invoked a force majeure clause following a fire at a processing facility, requiring the council to fund additional processing costs to maintain service. While the council found budget headroom to accommodate this, the incident illustrates the contract's exposure to market volatility and external shocks. The waste budget carries inherent volatility from global recycling markets.
findings.matters: Waste contracts are one of the largest council expenditures. Unexpected costs (£0.373m underspend in 2024/25 reversed to potential overspend) can consume reserves quickly. This is a specific recent incident showing real risk in a major budget line.
findings.figures: 2024/25 waste underspend £0.373m, 2025/26 quarter 3 underspend £0.219m, force majeure costs unknown but within budget headroom (Risk 12, para 3.18)
findings.quote: Following a recent fire at the Councils waste recycling contractor's processing plant the waste provider has enacted their business continuity plan, which was a seamless transfer from one processing plant to another. This created an immediate problem financially for the provider and they served a force majeure notice on the Council.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Homelessness and supported accommodation demand pressures unabated; additional budget headroom needed for growth in supported accommodation units
findings.detail: The council has experienced rising homelessness workload requiring permanent additional staff (previously temporary). Supported accommodation costs could increase by up to £0.229m if new units provided by private landlords become occupied. The council has budgeted for only 50% of this potential pressure. Homelessness demand is expected to increase in the foreseeable future with limited move-on accommodation available.
findings.matters: These are demand-led pressures outside the council's control. If supported accommodation units become occupied, the council will breach its budget or need reserve drawdown. This risk will transfer to the new unitary authority.
findings.figures: Potential additional supported accommodation cost £0.229m; budgeted provision 50% = £0.114m. Homelessness grant increased from £0.356m to £0.506m (Risk 11, para 4.31)
findings.quote: The Council is aware of potential growth in supported accommodation units provided by private landlords in the Borough, which if fully occupied could increase costs by up to £0.229m although the exact costs may vary. There is no expectation that demand for service will decrease in the foreseeable future with limited availability of move on accommodation.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Core Spending Power per capita of £134 is in the lowest 9% of district councils despite Fair Funding Review improvements
findings.detail: While Erewash benefited substantially from the FFR (CSP up 7.4% to £15.864m), its per-capita funding position remains weak. The council's CSP per capita of £134 ranks 142 out of 164 districts and is well below the £168 average. This indicates the council remains under-resourced relative to the average district despite the FFR being designed to address inequality.
findings.matters: Under-resourced councils relative to their needs often struggle with demand-led pressures (homelessness, supported accommodation) and face structural deficits that cannot be closed by efficiency alone. The low per-capita position suggests ongoing financial stress post-LGR.
findings.figures: CSP per capita £134 (2026/27), district average £166, Erewash rank 142/164 councils. CSP per capita 2025/26: £130; 2027/28: £141; 2028/29: £146 (para 4.22, Table 6)
findings.quote: In 2026/27 Erewash's CSP per capita of £134 is in the lowest 9% out of all districts and is well below the average of £168.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: £2.5m of the 2026/27 surplus is contingent on EPR funding of £1.839m which is volatile and not guaranteed beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: Extended Producer Responsibility (packaging waste) funding exceeded expectations by £1.2m at budget setting, delivering £1.839m for 2026/27 vs. £0.625m forecast a year ago. However, this funding is based on producer behaviour and will decline as packaging is reduced. The 2027/28 forecast assumes a 10% reduction. A material portion of the council's improved position depends on this non-guaranteed funding stream.
findings.matters: The council's headline 'no budget gap' position relies significantly on EPR income that could reduce or cease. Loss of EPR funding would require equivalent savings or reserve drawdown. This is outside the council's control.
findings.figures: 2026/27 EPR allocation £1.839m, 2027/28 forecast £1.650m (reduced by ~10%), 2028/29 forecast £1.350m (para 4.12, Table 7)
findings.quote: The Council received a provisional notification in November 2024 that EPR funding for 2025/26 would be £0.694m...the Council made additional representations, and it was acknowledged that an error has been made in the calculations which may increase the total figure by a further c£0.250m-£0.350m...the budget has therefore been set at this level, which is £1.214m more than when the 2025/26 budget was set.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Transition costs for Local Government Reorganisation potentially £1.5m but capped at £2.0m reserve allocation
findings.detail: The council is in transition to a new unitary authority. Government has not confirmed how much councils must contribute to shadow authority and integration costs. Erewash's share could be up to £1.5m, and the council has set aside a total of £2.0m in an LGR reserve. The council's own submission identified potential transition costs of c£50 million across all parties involved.
findings.matters: This is a material uncommitted cost for a new authority on day one. If the government requires higher contributions, the council may need to borrow or deplete further reserves. The uncertainty around costs and timing is substantial.
findings.figures: Potential Erewash share £1.5m, LGR reserve allocated £2.0m (including £0.5m already agreed for additional capacity) (Risk 15, para 5.44)
findings.quote: The submission made by the Council itself identifies potential transition costs of c£50 million. The government expectation is that each Council will contribute to these costs, but details have not been agreed locally. The share for Erewash could be £1.5m should the government not provide additional funding.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budget 202627 and Council Tax Report
findings.headline: Projected deficits of £0.420m (2027/28) and £1.120m (2028/29) timed exactly at Local Government Reorganisation vesting day
findings.detail: The council faces small deficits in 2027/28 and a material £1.120m deficit in 2028/29, coinciding with the expected 1 April 2028 vesting date for a new unitary authority. The council has set aside £2.365m in a Financial Sustainability Reserve to cover both deficits and unknown future pressures. However, the timing of these deficits means they transfer to the new authority at handover.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the new unitary will inherit £1.120m of deficit funding need in its first year. The FSR depletion pattern shows reserves running to near-zero by March 2028 except for £0.022m (para 5.45, Table 19).
findings.figures: 2027/28 deficit £0.420m, 2028/29 deficit £1.120m, FSR total available £2.365m (para 2.1(d), para 5.44)
findings.quote: the Council is projecting a provisional financial gap in 2027/28 of £0.420m and a gap of £1.120m in 2028/29 (Section 4 Table 8)

findings.headline: Revenue budget pressures are preventing the council from using revenue to fund capital projects
findings.detail: Council notes that while revenue resources could theoretically fund capital, 'pressures on the revenue budget limits the availability to fund schemes from this resource.' This indicates underlying revenue stress and loss of funding flexibility.
findings.matters: Revenue pressures restrict the tools available to manage capital needs and may indicate service delivery stress or efficiency challenges.
findings.figures: None specified.
findings.quote: The Council can also use revenue resources to fund capital projects, although pressures on the revenue budget limits the availability to fund schemes from this resource.

findings.headline: Council currently debt-free but acknowledges future borrowing may be needed and would strain the revenue budget
findings.detail: Council states it 'does not undertake any prudential borrowing' at present but recognises that 'if the need arose in the future, then any borrowing would need to be tightly controlled due to the financial impact it would have on the revenue budget.' This signals both future borrowing risk and acknowledged revenue constraints.
findings.matters: A transition from debt-free to borrowing status marks a material change in credit profile; the council's own language suggests revenue is tight enough that borrowing would create affordability pressure.
findings.figures: Currently zero borrowing; no amount specified for future scenario.
findings.quote: Although the Council currently does not undertake any prudential borrowing, if the need arose in the future, then any borrowing would need to be tightly controlled due to the financial impact it would have on the revenue budget.

findings.headline: Council depends on surplus land disposals for capital funding; if sales do not complete, must seek alternative financing including possible borrowing
findings.detail: Council approved disposal of multiple surplus land parcels (January 2023, November 2023, January 2024) and explicitly flags that if these sales do not realise receipts, it will have to consider other methods of financing—notably borrowing—in future. This creates execution risk and a contingent borrowing trigger.
findings.matters: Real estate sales are uncertain; if they do not complete, the council faces a financing gap and may be forced into prudential borrowing, which would affect revenue budget and credit profile.
findings.figures: Multiple parcels approved for disposal across three Executive meetings.
findings.quote: If capital receipts from land sales are not realised, then it will mean that the Council will have to consider other methods of financing capital expenditure in the future.

findings.headline: Council is asset-light and cannot realise significant capital receipts to fund investment
findings.detail: Erewash explicitly states it is 'not asset rich' and that 'the ability to realise significant capital receipts is becoming limited'. This is the primary constraint on capital spending: with no near-term borrowing plans and limited external funding, the council has restricted capacity to invest beyond what grants and contributions cover.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how a council can fund capital to maintain and improve assets; a council unable to realise receipts from disposals faces constraints on service investment and debt capacity.
findings.figures: Not specified; capacity depends on land sales.
findings.quote: However, the Council is not asset rich and the ability to realise significant capital receipts is becoming limited.

findings.headline: Financial statements will be published without audit opinion per statutory requirement
findings.detail: The Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations 2024 require the council to publish its accounts by 27 February 2026 even though an audit opinion cannot be issued. Unverified financial information will be released as the council's official statement of accounts.
findings.matters: Lenders often covenant on receipt of audited accounts or require audit opinion compliance. Publication of disclaimed-audit accounts signals governance breakdown and typically triggers review of lending terms or covenant defaults.
findings.figures: Publication deadline: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: The Council is required to publish its Accountability Statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, by 27 February 2026 ('the 2026 backstop date').

findings.headline: Rebuilding assurance cannot be completed even using NAO recovery guidance
findings.detail: Auditors reviewed the NAO's Local Audit Reset and Recovery Guidance (LARRIG 06) but concluded there is not sufficient time to complete the procedures they deem necessary to rebuild assurance by the 27 February 2026 backstop date. Standard recovery guidance is inadequate for this council's situation.
findings.matters: If recovery procedures outlined by the NAO are insufficient, this signals deeper structural problems in the audit trail. Lenders face an indefinite period during which no verified financial information about the council will be available.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 27 February 2026; earliest possible recovery: 2026/27 or later
findings.quote: We have determined that there is not sufficient time to carry out the procedures we deem necessary to rebuild assurance. As a result, we are not able obtain sufficient appropriate evidence upon which to form an opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 before the 2026 backstop date.

findings.headline: No substantive testing performed on any balance or transaction in the accounts
findings.detail: Due to the backstop date, auditors did not test any of the numbers reported in the financial statements. Not a single balance or transaction was verified through audit procedures. No misstatements were found because no testing was done to find them.
findings.matters: Substantive testing is how auditors verify financial numbers are real and correct. Untested figures are, from a lender's perspective, unverified claims without evidence. This makes formal credit assessment impossible.
findings.figures: All balances and transactions: zero substantive testing
findings.quote: Due to the backstop, we have not undertaken substantive testing procedures on any balances or transactions reported in the accounts.

findings.headline: No assurance over opening balances cascades through current year accounts
findings.detail: Because prior-year audits were disclaimed, auditors have no verified starting position for 2024/25 balances. This breaks the audit chain: without confirming what the council started with, they cannot audit what it ended with. The current year's financial position is built on unverified foundations.
findings.matters: Lenders assess trends and changes in council finances. Without confirmed opening balances, any apparent change in financial position or reserve movements cannot be verified or trusted.
findings.figures: Opening balances for year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We do not have assurance over the opening balances in the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.headline: Third consecutive audit disclaimer — no verified financial statements for three years
findings.detail: Erewash has received disclaimed audit opinions for 2022/23 (by EY), 2023/24, and 2024/25 (both by Forvis Mazars). A disclaimer means auditors express no opinion and provide zero assurance on the financial statements. No lender can assess creditworthiness from unaudited accounts spanning three years.
findings.matters: Lenders require verified financial statements to assess credit risk and council solvency. Without audited accounts, lending decisions are made blind and loan covenants typically require audit opinion compliance.
findings.quote: We issued a disclaimed opinion on your financial statements for 2023/24 financial year. We also note that the predecessor auditors, Ernst & Young LLP, issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements for the 2022/23 financial year.

news_drafts.headline: From 1 April 2027, the council will restrict permanent recruitment to essential posts only; senior management will shift to temporary or shared arrangements
news_drafts.lead: Severe restrictions on recruitment and temporary management structures during final transition months create operational risk - reduced institutional knowledge, potential service continuity issues, and limited decision-making capacity at a critical time.

news_drafts.headline: From late 2026/early 2027, a Section 24 regime will require Shadow Council consent for major financial commitments above set thresholds
news_drafts.lead: Section 24 restrictions could delay or prevent necessary financial or capital decisions during the critical transition period, reducing operational flexibility when it is most needed. Their imposition also signals government concern about financial…

news_drafts.headline: The council will rely on drawing down the Financial Sustainability Reserve to cover projected budget deficits rather than making structural spending adjustments
news_drafts.lead: Using reserves to fund ongoing deficits is unsustainable - it masks structural problems rather than solving them, potentially forcing abrupt decisions on the new unitary council immediately after vesting if the FSR is insufficient.
